etymology.text: 计 ‘to count, to calculate’ + 划 ‘to plan, to mark out’. Attested in Classical Chinese, and popularized from Japanese 計画 (keikaku) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: 计划 is one of many modern words that Chinese and Japanese share: 計画 keikaku.
pitfalls: Taiwan writes 計畫, Hong Kong and many older texts 計劃 — both are correct traditional spellings.
subtleties: 计划 sounds organised, often written down; for a simple personal intention people say 打算: 你明天有什么打算？

tradPerSense.none: traditional 計劃 for every sense (Taiwan’s standard spelling is 計畫)

toneSandhi.none: no 一 or 不 in the word

etymology.text: 打 ‘to hit; to do’ + 算 ‘to calculate’: ‘work out the sums’ — to reckon, to plan.

funFacts: 打 is the ‘do’ of many verbs: 打电话 ‘make a phone call’, 打球 ‘play ball’, 打算 ‘make plans’.
pitfalls: 打算 + verb needs no word for ‘to’: 我打算去. The negative is 不打算 ‘don’t intend to’ or 没打算 ‘hadn’t planned to’.
subtleties: 打算 tells an intention, not a certainty: 我打算去 ‘I mean to go’, 我会去 ‘I will go’, 我要去 ‘I’m going (it’s decided)’.

etymology.text: 酒 ‘wine, liquor’ + 店 ‘shop’. Wiktionary still lists the senses ‘bar, tavern’ and ‘liquor shop’; today the word means above all ‘hotel’.

funFacts: 北京饭店 ‘Beijing Hotel’ is a hotel, not a restaurant: 饭店 in a name is often a hotel.
pitfalls: 酒店 is not a bar: a bar is 酒吧 (jiǔbā). In Taiwan 酒店 can also mean a hostess club — 饭店 or 旅馆 is safer there.
subtleties: Staying at a hotel is 住酒店 / 住在酒店 (住 ‘to live, to stay’).

etymology.text: 预 ‘in advance’ + 订 ‘to fix, to agree on’: ‘fix in advance’.

funFacts: 预 ‘in advance’ is also in 预报 ‘forecast’ (天气预报 ‘weather forecast’).
pitfalls: 预订 ‘to book’ and 预定 ‘to fix beforehand, scheduled’ are both yùdìng — the characters are often mixed up.
subtleties: In speech the short 订 is more common (订酒店, 订票); 预订 is the word of websites and hotel desks.

etymology.text: 护 ‘to protect’ + 照 ‘licence, certificate’ (as in 驾照 ‘driving licence’): ‘a protecting document’.

funFacts: 照 also means ‘photo’ (照片) — and every 护照 has one.
pitfalls: Getting a passport is 办护照 ‘handle a passport’, not *买护照.
subtleties: A passport is counted like a book: 一本护照.

funFacts: 行 has two readings: xíng ‘to go’ (行李, 旅行) and háng ‘row, trade’ (银行 ‘bank’).
pitfalls: Luggage itself (行李) is counted with 件: 两件行李; a 行李箱 is counted with 个.

funFacts: Order matters: 国外 ‘outside the country’ = abroad; 外国 ‘outside country’ = a foreign country.
pitfalls: 国外 is a place, 外国 a country: 在国外 ‘abroad’, but 外国人 ‘a foreigner’ — not *国外人.
subtleties: 国外 behaves like a place name: 在国外, 去国外, 从国外.

etymology.text: 出 ‘to go out’ + 国 ‘country’: ‘go out of the country’; Wiktionary writes it 出⫽國 (separable).

funFacts: Its opposite is 回国 ‘to return to one’s own country’.
pitfalls: 出国 takes no object: ‘go to France’ is 去法国, not *出国法国.
subtleties: 过 goes inside: 我没出过国 ‘I have never been abroad’.

etymology.text: 参 ‘to join, to take part’ + 观 ‘to look at’: ‘join in and look’.

funFacts: A sign saying 谢绝参观 means ‘no visitors’.
pitfalls: 参观 is for places and things, never for people: visiting a friend is 看朋友 / 看望朋友.
subtleties: 参观 is looking round as a visitor; staying somewhere is not 参观: *参观北京三天 → 在北京玩三天.

tànwàng: visit (especially the sick)

etymology.text: 看 ‘to look, to see’ + 望 ‘to look into the distance; to visit’: ‘go and see someone’.

funFacts: Visiting the sick with fruit or flowers is usual — but never with a clock: 送钟 ‘give a clock’ sounds like 送终 ‘attend a deathbed’.
pitfalls: 看望 is for people (family, the sick, older people), not for places: visiting a museum is 参观.
subtleties: 看望 sounds caring and respectful — a visit to someone older, ill or far away.

guānguāngkè: tourist (common in Taiwan)

etymology.text: 游 ‘to roam, to tour’ + 客 ‘guest, visitor’.

funFacts: 客 ‘guest’ makes many words for people: 客人 ‘guest’, 乘客 ‘passenger’, 顾客 ‘customer’.
pitfalls: A passenger on a train or a plane is 乘客 or 旅客, not 游客 — a 游客 is there to look round.
subtleties: 游客 is often said of the crowd; one visitor, politely, is 一位游客.

etymology.text: 导 ‘to lead, to guide’ + 游 ‘to tour’: ‘the one who leads the tour’. Wiktionary also lists the verb ‘to conduct a tour’.

funFacts: 导 ‘lead’ also gives 导演 ‘film director’ and 导师 ‘tutor, supervisor’.
pitfalls: A guidebook is not 导游 but 旅游指南 (lǚyóu zhǐnán).
subtleties: 导游 is the person and the job: 他做导游 ‘he works as a guide’.

etymology.text: 下 ‘below; next’ + 星期 ‘week’: in Chinese, time runs downwards — 上 is before, 下 after.

funFacts: 上个月 ‘last month’, 下个月 ‘next month’: earlier time is ‘up’, later time ‘down’.
pitfalls: 下星期一 is ‘next Monday’: 下 goes before the whole day name (*星期一下 is wrong).
subtleties: 下星期 and 下个星期 mean the same; 个 makes it a little more colloquial.

funFacts: With 周 the weekdays are short too: 周一 … 周日 (S14) — so 下周三 is ‘next Wednesday’.
pitfalls: Traditional characters write the week 週 (下週); 周 alone is also the Zhou dynasty, which keeps 周.
subtleties: 下周 is compact and neutral — the form of timetables, e-mails and the news.

etymology.text: 明 ‘bright; next (of days and years)’ + 年 ‘year’ — like 明天 ‘tomorrow’.

funFacts: The series: 前年 ‘the year before last’, 去年 ‘last year’, 今年 ‘this year’, 明年 ‘next year’, 后年 ‘the year after next’.
pitfalls: Next month and next week take 下 (下个月, 下星期), but next year is 明年 — not *下年.
subtleties: 明年 is a time word: before the verb, with no preposition (我明年去).

lexemes.role: will — the future of prediction, 明天会很冷 (C03); ‘can’ (a learned skill) is taught with the modal verbs (C05)

synonyms.nuance: yào: be going to — something decided or near

jiāng: will

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 合 ‘to meet’ + a phonetic part. Wiktionary derives its readings from one root ‘to join, to come together ~ to meet ~ to fit ~ to understand’.

funFacts: ‘Come together’ → ‘meet’, ‘meeting’; ‘understand’ → ‘know how’ → ‘will’: Wiktionary links the meanings of 会 to one root.
pitfalls: 不会 is both ‘won’t’ and ‘can’t (never learnt)’: 他不会来 ‘he won’t come’, 他不会游泳 ‘he can’t swim’ — the verb and the situation decide.
subtleties: 会 predicts (it will probably happen); 要 announces (it is decided or near): 明天会很冷, but 我明天要走 ‘I’m leaving tomorrow’.

readings.none: huì in every sense here; kuài only in 会计 ‘accounting’, another word

toneSandhi.none: no 一 or 不 in the word
